https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-assis.text: LONDON — Britain is still lagging behind Australia when it comes to assisted dying. But one Labour MP who has seen the debate in both countries is hoping she can push forward a thwarted attempt at change in the U.K. “If I had six months to live and I was facing a potentially very frightening, very painful, very uncomfortable death, I would want to be able to have the choice to choose to end my life surrounded by my family,” Lauren Edwards, who became an MP in 2024 — and hails from Melbourne, Australia, tells POLITICO in an interview. Edwards’ support for assisted dying is shaped in part by the laws in Victoria, where she still has family. In 2017, it became the first Australian state to legalize assisted dying for people expected to die within six months, or 12 months for those with neurodegenerative diseases, and who face unacceptable suffering. Advertisement Advertisement Though Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model — unbearable suffering is not a criterion for eligibility in her bill — she found it helpful to see how assisted dying has worked in practice the last time British MPs tackled this issue. It’s an experience from which many in Labour still bear the scars — and on which new Prime Minister Andy Burnham already appears to have drawn a line in the sand. Stepping forward MPs passed fellow Labour backbencher Kim Leadbeater’s Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill last year by 314 votes to 291. But it failed to become law after delays in the U.K.’s House of Lords. Now Edwards is reintroducing the bill — and is adamant that the groundbreaking social change can succeed this time around. It means that next month, the House of Commons will once again be thrust into a divisive vote on a matter of conscience, deciding whether to legalize assisted dying in England and Wales for terminally ill adults judged as having fewer than six months left to live. “When Kim’s bill came up, I did have conversations with my dad about how things have gone in Australia,” Edwards says. The situation reassured her compared to “more extreme examples” like Canada, where a terminal condition is not required for patients to be eligible, but instead an irreversible, “advanced state of decline” and “unbearable physical or mental suffering.” Advertisement Advertisement Next year, Canadian eligibility for assisted dying is set to be expanded to include individuals whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness, though this change has been repeatedly delayed. Sense-checking the legislation with family down under was “really important” when weighing up whether to support Leadbeater’s earlier proposals, she says. Edwards has Australian friends who have settled in Britain too — and contrasts a friend able to attend his mother’s assisted death in Australia with British families currently worried about prosecution for helping relatives to die. U.K. law punishes the offense with up to 14 years in prison. Lauren Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model. | House of Commons “[The] status quo is not neutral. It is not benign,” Edwards argues. “It is a situation where, if we don’t make this legislative change, unfortunately, we will be allowing that pain, fear and isolation.” In October 2024, an independent review of assisted dying in Victoria by the state Department of Health’s Centre for Evaluation and Research Evidence found the system to be safe and “operating as intended” with “no reports of ineligible individuals” accessing substances to end their lives. However, access to assisted dying varies across the vast state — which is only slightly smaller than the entire U.K. — and just “a few practitioners” deliver the majority of care. Victoria has been urged to press the central Australian government for more funding. Advertisement Advertisement Choice of priorities Back in the U.K., the main political parties have agreed that the decision to legalize assisted dying should be a matter for parliament, rather than any one administration. MPs were not whipped to vote in any particular way on Leadbeater’s bill, and the issue is treated as a matter of conscience. But there was tacit endorsement for the most recent attempted overhaul from the top of Keir Starmer’s government. Before entering No. 10, Starmer promised broadcaster Esther Rantzen — who has stage four lung cancer — that he’d make time for a vote in parliament. Leadbeater’s bill also received technical support from civil servants in the Department for Health and Social Care and the Ministry of Justice to ensure its workability. New Prime Minister Andy Burnham appears to have other ideas. Burnham was not an MP when assisted dying passed the Commons last year and abstained in a 2015 vote during a previous stint in parliament. More strikingly, when asked about his stance on the issue last month, Burnham said “the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care” needs to happen first — and argued it would be “very challenging” to introduce assisted dying without substantial progress on these two running policy sores. Edwards remains bullish. She commends the PM’s commitment to sustainably funding social care — Burnham has kicked off cross-party talks on the issue and asked for a speedier inquiry — and she insists his professed skepticism hasn’t put her off. Advertisement Advertisement “It’s really important that we consider them together,” Edwards says of social care and assisted dying. “I don’t think that there is a reason to delay” changing the law, she argues, highlighting £125 million provided by Starmer’s government for adult and children’s hospices. (A Public Accounts Committee report said this one-off funding did not directly pay for service delivery or solve financial problems facing the sector.) Edwards’ bill has a four-year implementation period. That means if it becomes law next year, assisted dying wouldn’t be permitted until 2031. She believes the two systems can work on a “dual track” and that poor palliative care won’t incentivize people to access assisted dying. “I don’t necessarily think that lack of care is a motivator for this option,” she argues. “I think it’s a last resort when physical suffering really can’t be relieved.” Yvette Cooper speaks during a visit to a care home in London on July 29, 2026. | Pool photo by Kirsty Wigglesworth via WPA/Getty Images From MPs to peers A majority of Starmer’s Cabinet backed the bill last time, including Health Secretary Yvette Cooper and Justice Secretary Alex Norris — but only 12 MPs need to switch sides for the bill to fall, making the margins tight. Indeed, suspended Labour MP Karl Turner told POLITICO he’ll vote against the bill after abstaining last June. “People’s views are largely what I expect them to be when we next vote on this,” Edwards argues. “We haven’t seen any significant moves away from people who were supportive of the bill.” Then there is the substantive question of the House of Lords. Edwards condemns the “small minority” of peers she blames for filibustering the previous bill. She said she is happy to work with peers on good faith amendments in the “scrutiny process” this time around. Advertisement Advertisement The pro-assisted dying camp will be relying on a little-used pair of laws — the Parliament Acts — which would, in narrow circumstances, allow a bill to be passed despite being deadlocked or defeated by peers in the House of Lords again. “I want to get it back to [peers] ASAP so that they will have the maximum amount of time to finish the job of scrutinizing,” Edwards says. An impassioned opposition campaign last time around argued Leadbeater’s bill was not safe. The Royal College of Psychiatrists , while neutral on the principle of assisted dying, said it could not support her plans due to a lack of clarity about their profession’s role in the process and whether adequate resources are in place. While Edwards may struggle to win over Burnham, she hopes to “sit down and have a conversation” with the prime minister before MPs return from recess in September. One open question remains: how Starmer himself will vote. As prime minister, he voted for it, but didn’t explain his reasoning. Now freed from the constraints of government, Edwards hopes Starmer will make an intervention. “He has a well-known legal background, is very considered and is obviously a really crucial voice,” she says. Starmer’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

https://theconversation.com/can-governme.text: Skip to content Hinterhaus Productions/Getty https://theconversation.com/can-governments-ever-convince-women-to-have-more-babies-heres-what-other-countries-can-teach-us-292903 https://theconversation.com/can-governments-ever-convince-women-to-have-more-babies-heres-what-other-countries-can-teach-us-292903 Link copied Share article Share article Copy link Email Bluesky Facebook WhatsApp Messenger LinkedIn X (Twitter) Print article Australia will see more deaths than births by the 2060s according to the Intergenerational Report released by the treasurer last week. Two trends are working together: Australians are living longer and having fewer babies. Birthrates are falling everywhere on Earth. Only one developed country has enough children to replace its adults: Israel , with its singularly child-focused culture. Australia’s birthrates are about middle of the pack, with 1.48 children per woman. But if Australia’s births continue at this rate, the population will age and shrink. The question is whether the government has a role in either extending lifespans or increasing births, and what that role should be. Parenting advocate Georgie Dent used a speech at the National Press Club to suggest some ways the government might relieve the burden of parenting: long paid parental leave, affordable child care and child-friendly employment. But would these policies encourage young people to start a family? Would they nudge a couple to have one more child? Luckily, we have a rich array of data on family-friendly policies from around the world to assess whether government strategies like these can actually encourage people to have children. Hungary’s short-lived success Hungary and the Nordic countries have remarkable pro-natal benefits. In 2011, Hungary had an alarmingly low birthrate of 1.23 children per woman. The country’s leaders reacted with a multi-pronged plan , including: cash payments for marriages and births subsidised loans that are forgiven as family size increases tax relief that increases by number of children, with women having four or more children exempt from tax for life a car subsidy affordable child care. Hungary did not achieve replacement fertility, but with these investments, it seemed to be getting closer, climbing to 1.63 children per woman by 2021. After that, births started dropping, and by 2025, there were 1.31 births per woman. The speed and severity of the drop surprised observers. One theory is that Hungary’s family benefits encouraged women to change the timing of births they would have had anyway. When that temporary acceleration of births ended, one of the most comprehensive pro-natalist programs in the world landed Hungary in the same place it had been before the laws changed. What about the Nordic countries? The Nordic countries – Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Finland and Iceland – have rich, stable economies, high employment and cradle-to-grave welfare systems. Their pro-family policies have been sustained over several decades. They are designed to make it less expensive to have a child, and to encourage egalitarian division of labour between mothers and fathers at home and at work. All the Nordic countries have generous parental leave schemes, with Norway being highest ranked in the world, offering almost a year at 100% pay, which can be shared between parents. Sweden offers 15 months at 80% pay. Norway, Iceland, Sweden and Denmark are also top-ranked globally for child care , which is heavily subsidised and can be at home or in a formal setting. The Nordic countries’ pursuit of gender equity means that the burden for women at home is reduced. By encouraging women to stay in the workforce, the adverse effect on women’s income and wealth is diminished. Altogether, the Nordic countries are the gold standard in parental leave, child care, father involvement and mother career success. Until 2010, their birthrates were also significantly higher than most of the developed world. And then, after 2010, something changed. Birthrates declined by about 20–30% simultaneously in the Nordics. The biggest change is that women are resisting having a first child. How is this possible? The most generous, egalitarian countries on the planet were able to keep their births high despite the decline in the rest of the world. But now, they, too, have falling birthrates, which are now around the same or lower than Australia’s. Why has this happened? There is no agreed-upon answer. Women’s dreams for an adequate standard of living to start a family might be inflating faster than even the best government benefits. Or it may be that no amount of money can convince a woman to have a child. She may be waiting for the perfect moment, or the perfect partner, or she may be choosing another path in life. Read more: How much does it really cost to raise a child? An expert does the maths So why do women have children? In my research , I have been talking to women who have four or more children. When they explain why they have children, they talk about what gives them meaning. They talk about continuity, about family and community. Most women want to parent with a partner, someone who will get up in the night and also be making breakfast in the morning. Someone who shares their values and their sacrifices. As a result, women are getting increasingly choosy about who they want to spend their lives with . They’d rather be without a partner, and without children, than make the imperfect choice. Can governments encourage births? There is nostalgia for the Peter Costello-era baby cash bonus in Australia in the 2000s, which gave a $3,000 lump sum payment to new parents. It did increase births, but probably, like in Hungary, only by changing the timing of births that would otherwise have happened anyway. Study after study shows government policies can change the timing of births, and even shift birthrates at the margin. But no policy has been able to raise births to replacement levels in the long term. There are good reasons to support paid parental leave and affordable daycare, but they are not likely to motivate women to start a family. For that, women need to have a good partner, a supportive family and a community. That’s probably more than we can ask elected officials to provide. The president of Poland, Karol Nawrocki, will hold a closed-door meeting next week for talks about the country’s bid to obtain another permanent U.S. base. (Emilie Lenglain/U.S. Army) By JOHN VANDIVER STARS AND STRIPES Published October 29, 2026 · Poland’s president has called a meeting with senior national security officials next week to discuss efforts aimed at attracting a new permanent U.S. military base in the country . President Karol Nawrocki will hold the closed-door meeting Tuesday in Warsaw, his National Security Bureau announced this week. The meeting comes as Polish officials prepare proposals for the Pentagon detailing basing options in the country. Warsaw has said it is prepared to pay for a new base, which could cost between $3 billion and $4 billion. If the two countries agree on the terms, that could mean 5,000 more troops residing in Poland on a permanent basis. Most U.S. troops currently assigned there are on temporary rotational missions. Polish officials have said they hope to eventually have a mix of 10,000 rotational troops and 5,000 permanent ones. Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said Wednesday that the proposed American installation would be a central topic of Tuesday’s meeting. Poland has identified four potential locations for a base, all in the western part of the country. The selected cities are Wroclaw, Poznan, Bydgoszcz and Szczecin, Kosiniak-Kamysz said in an interview last week with the Polish news outlet WNP. Plans for a new base in Poland have been gaining momentum. While the Pentagon is currently wrapping up a force posture review that could include troop reductions in Europe, Poland has been a priority for the U.S. military. In September, President Donald Trump said Washington and Warsaw are making progress toward a new basing deal. “If this happens, the location will be announced very soon,” Trump said on Truth Social. “This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.” Also in September, a U.S. delegation visited Poland to inspect possible locations for a permanent American base. While the U.S. Army already has a small permanent base in Poznan, most of the military sites used by American troops in Poland are austere locations designed to serve rotational contingents. Establishing a major permanent base would entail building family housing, schools and the other amenities typically required to support troops and their families. NATO Poland John Vandiver covers U.S. military activities across Europe and Africa. Based in Stuttgart, Germany, he previously worked for newspapers in New Jersey, North Carolina and Maryland. He is a graduate of the University of Delaware.
